ATROCITIES IN BULGA.R.IA. MEETING AT ALTRINOHAM.

IA crowded meeting MIS held on Wednesday evening An the Town Hall, Alttincham. The chair was "cuPied by Ed. Neild,Esst., the Illayor of Altrincham, Who remarked that the meeting had been called in IPpporge to a requisition numerously and influentially Signed.

Mr. W. Maws then moved the following resolution ."`" That this meeting hereby records its detestation of the crimes which have disgraced Turkish tyranny in the war now raging in Turkish territory, and calls upon the English Government to use all the influence it possesses to atop these atrocities, and to adopt effectual cleans for securing the Christian subjects of Turkey from the ty,nnny and barbarism of their Mahom. medan lsr,. ' tie did not regard the question as in any way a political one, but as one of common humanity. He thought the power of England in the councils of Turkey was greater than the power of any other country. England had a special right to be heard, and to use its influence in this matter—a right to say that we will not permit these atrocities, and that If they are continued England will withdraw all sup- Port from the Turkish Government. What is wanted Is that our Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary be Stirred up to the belief that the English people insist that our fellow Christians in those States of Turkey 0241 be liberated from the cruel and devilish dominion exercised over them by the Turkish power. The Rev. W. Rasmus, who sessonded the resolution though t that Turkey was incurable in the way of cupidity: cruelty, lust, and perfidy. When I think—he said— of the bleaching_bones in Bulgaria; of the perfidy of the Turkish Government for years and centuries past; the repeated outbreaks of torture and butchery of the men, women, and children torn from their homes and destroyed; and that the Turkish Government has re- Warded the principal instruments in this carnage, I say, down with the rule of the Turk, and let the op. Pressed go free. The Rev.-T. ADAMSON supported the resolution. He thought that if rulers and warriors would not put a Stop to these awful outrages, we in this country must Lift up our voices and try to put an eternal stop to them.

The resolution was unanimously adopted: Mr. E. Bons moved the following resolution" That his Worship the Mayor be requested to forward to the Prime Minister and to the Earl of Derby a copy of the previous resolution. He did not knew to whom the blame of the continuance of these outrages was to be attributed, but he felt sure that records of meetings Such as these would find their way to the proper quarter. The whole syetem of Turkey was rotten and Should be swept away, and he was certain that when the voice of this country had been heard there would be a different state of things in Constantinople. (A question. What is your remedy.) Mr. W. ABMITIGE seconded the resolution. A ques- tion had been asked. What is your remedy ? The remedy is simple. We have spent our money and shed Our blood to keep these Turks in their present position, and to give them power over those countries which have been so barbarously treated. Let our country lay this must be stopped ; if not there is an end of our treaties, and there can beno doubt that if England turns Its back upon Turkey, Turkey will soon have to turn Its back upon itself. Mr. W. H. PA.BICES supported the resolution. He deplored the condition into whieh Turkey bad fallen. It was a °country of vast rummies, of large population, and of much intelligence, and he felt certain that if stringent methods were adopted a great reformation in the character of its people might take place. The Rev. E. Weinwziour thought it a mistake to Make political capital out of this question, and he Should be sorry to think any party was trying to do so. Any Government in power at a critical period must not be too thin-skinned, too sensitive, and any Govern tient in aloe sae ready to find fault when out o. office, and each must take their share. When Cowart vatives complained that the country was looking at this question from a party point of view, they mus bear in mind that the country was looking at it in Way which was unavoidable and quite natural. Let Turkey know that we will no longer fraternise with it, and it will have a marvellous influence on its future

acts. The resolution was carried with soolamation. It was then moved by Mr. P. Brxxort, seconded and resolved that the following be appended to the terms Cif the first resolution, "that it entirely exclude their administration over the dominions of _Bosnia, Benda, lind lie' regains. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Mr. W. Milne, and seconded by Sir. Davison, brought the proceedings to a close.

AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

The fifteenth annual show was hold on Friday and Saturday. Though the show may fairly be said to have been a successful one, yet as a pecuniary success It was far behind its predecessors. The awards of prises to local exhibitors must be a source of !Adidas. tion to the people of Altrinoham, an evidence that the tradesmen of Altrincham are able to compete, and . _ .

that successfully, with any others in the country. Mr. George Bowen, of George-street. Altrincham—with. out whose exhibits no show at Altrincham would seem complete—was awarded the first prise, a silver cup or SS, for a general collection of agricultural machines and implements, whioh was open to general and not
district competition. Mr. A. Devonport, of the Downs, Altrincham, was awarded the second prize, value kg, Mr. David Harkes; of Mere, was awarded the first

- prize, £4, for collection of agricultural implements for tilling or field use. A first-class certificate was given to Mr. Geo. Richardson, George-street, Altrinoham, for a miscellaneous oolleotion of saddlery. The prize for turn-outs in the list was won by Mr. 3. S. Milne, Sale ; and in the competition open to all England for pony turn-outs, a special prize was awarded to Mr. T. P. Taylor, Lymm. The Mayor of ,Altrincham (Mr. E. , Nield) won the special prize for peny turn-outs-- under 13 hands. The principal prize for jumping was carried off by Mr. J. Cousins, Sandiway, Northwich, with "Blue Peter," a somewhat celebrated jumper. Mr, T. P. Taylor took several prizes for root e ; 11r. John Owen, of Lymm, was also a prize taker in this class, but the principal prize was given to Mr. W. Bailie, Northenden. The chief prizes for sheep were as arded to Mr. John Markendale, of Dunham Massey. Amongst the prize takers for horses were Mr. W. Bellhousej3ale ; Mr. Sidney L. Keymer, Timperley ; Mr. B. Gads% Andric/tam ; Mr. J. M thendale, Mr. G. J. Carter, Tett= Dale; Mr. J. S. Milnes, Altrin- chain ;_ Mr. J. B. Newton, Sandiway, Altrineham ; and Mr. Wm. Derbyshire, Morris Brook. Amongst the takers of prizes for dogs were Mr. W'. Tootell, Northwich ; Mr. Wm. Pierpoint, Latchford; Mr. J. M. Rigby, Heatley ; Mr. L. H. Leyland, Morris Brook; Mr. T. Hurst, Tabley (commended); Mr. J. P. Cartwright, Brookfield, Lymm ; Mr. Wm. Moore, Northwich; Mr.R. Alston, Sale; Mr. R. I. Hartley, Dunham Massey ; Mr. J. Nicholson, Bowdon; and Mr. H. Crosby, Sale (highly commended). At the conclusion of the Show there was a luncheon at the "Unicorn Hotel, Altrineham, the Hon. Wilbra- ham Egerton, M.P., president of the society, occupied the chair. In response to the toast "The members for Mid-Cheshire," the Chairman expressed the interest he took in agriculture, and in all matters relating to the welfare of the agrionitnrists of the &minty. During the past semen they had not had no much in the way of measures affecting directly the agricultural interests, i as had been the case n former sessions. They had not been able, owing to want of time which lied been somewhat fruitlessly consumed in talking—to carry I such measures as the Highway Act, and the Prisons Act, bo h of which would have affected considerably agricultural interests. .The latter Bill especially would have been a relief to that local taxation which was now put upon county residents, to the extent of three- farthings in the pound, or a sum of between £7,000 and £B,OOO per annum. He trusted that next session the Bill would be re-introduced. It was a Bill which might very fairly be brought in, because it did not, he believed, interfere with that local self-government which was so valuable, and which should be preserved. As regarded the subject of education, he would only say on the present occasion that he believed the Bill which had just been passed would tend very largely to improve the education of the country, and mast benefit all classes, especially agriculturists, now that they required so much skilled labour. He trusted that the extension of education in the agricultural districts —although those districts at the present time were by no means behind the manufacturing districts—would raise the condition of the agricultural labourer, teach him the advantages of literary pursuits, give him during the long winter nights greater resources for instructing his mind, and so prevent him from resort- ing to that bad alternative, the public house. _ .

Mr. PIUS EfiliUTON-WAUDINUOrf_, M.P., also re. sponded. He said that although he had only had about one month in Parliament, he could not say that he found it altogether a bed of roses. Perhaps it would be presumptuous in him to make any complaints, or to find fault with that august body, but there were two things of which he must complain. One was that many members talked a great deal more than was ne- cessary—for he was sure they would do a great deal more work if there was less talking—and the other was the late hours at which members were kept up at night. He felt it a very great privilege, and one to which he should always look :back with pleasure, that he had been allowed to enter the House of Commons during the time when Mr. Disraeli was in power, and thus to listen to eloquence of a very high order. .4.11 men, of whatever politics, must, he was sure, feel that Mr. Disraeli had done a great deal of good for this country, and that he had justly deserved the great honour which had been conferred upon him. He (21r. Warburton) could not help saying that he regretted very deeply that some papers had tried to make poll. tint capital out of what were called the Bulgarian atrocities. Those atrocities had nothing to do with party, but formed altogether a national question-- a question of humanity, not of polities—and there- fore to make them into a political question wee a great mistake: The Government was the Government of the most humane country in the world, and it had done all that any Government, whether Liberal or Conservative, could do by remonstrating with the Ottoman Empire most strongly, and by using all its efforts to suppress the atrocities which had been com- mitted. He thought whatever humanity could sug- gest or a strong Government enforce had been done, and that it had been done so effectually that nothing more would be heard of them. No one had a greater horror of such atrocities than he had, but before we allowed our indignation to get the better of us—as he was afraid had been the case—we should remember that the Turks were trying to suppress an almost suc- cessful rebellion,. that their Sultan was deposed, and that they were in a state of internal discord. We must remember, also, before we condemned them too strongly, the example of terrible vengeeme vrlaioh w4e given them by our soldiers in the mutiny in India, and which perhaps was justified. We should make some little allowance for .1% lialf•uivilised nation, and before condemning them should remember a certain parable. in the Bible about "taking the mote out of thy brothe.'s eye."

Four men named William Sinicook, John Sinicook, Alfred Brown, and George Baker, were charged with committing a trespass at Sutton on land in the occupa- tion of Mrs. Hyde, farmer, on the 3rd inst. Mr. Lewin, of Widnes, appeared for the defendants. Jag. Turner, gamekeeper, said the defendants were am. ployed on the Louden and North Western Railway, one of them being a signalman. When watching the box from the field he saw the four men emerge from it with three dogs. He saw one of the dogs chasing a hare in the adjacent field. Mr. Lewin said that the men were summoned for "entering and being upon I land." As the men were not in the field at all he asked for the cases to be dismissed. Mr. Johnson, the deputy clerk, /minted out two cases to the Bench which showed that it had been held that when a dog jumped into a close with the incitement of his master a trespass had been committed. Mr. Lewin said there was no proof of the men having incited the dog, and the ease referred to was not a game trespass. A game trespass mat be personal and constructive. Consider. able discussion ensued on this point, and ultimately the Bench decided to give Mr. Lewin's clients the benefit of the technical objection raised, and dismissed the case, but at the same time stating that they were fully aware of the defendants intentions, although they had not been found M the commission of the act.

ON THE TURKISH QUESTION.

At a crowded and enthusiastic meeting, held in Warrington on Wednesday evening', in condemnation of the Turkish atrocities in Bulgaria, Mr. S. Rigby, IP., presiding, Mr. Rylinds, M.P., for Burnley, ad- dressed the meeting at. considerable length on the general question, and especially in reply to the recent ',pooch of Lord Derby.

Mr. Itneams, M.P., who, on rising, met with a most enthusiastic reception, said Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen, my friend Mr. Croafield has alluded to the fact that this , meeting has been called by the Liberal party and not by the Mayor, and I have heard certain leading Conservative members of the Town Council, who have complained to me, that the Liberal party should have given a party complexi n to this movement, and who have called this meeting, in. stead of calling it by a requisition to the Mayor. I can only say that if there had been a requieiton to the Mayor, and had the meeting been called, I should have sought, as a townsman of Warrington, to have been present at that meeting. (Cheers.) But I ask the question " Why was there not a requisition to the Mayor p- (Hear, hear, and cheers.) These leading Conservative members of the Town Council, aldermen, and others, were just the men to have headed the ree quisition to the Mayor, and I charge them with having shrunk from getting up a requisition to the Mayor, and , that we, as ri Liberal party, have been called upon, in consequence of the absence of any general movement, to take this opportunity of protesting in the voice of the town, and in the absence of the Mayor, against the most grievous crime that has ever been committed by the British Government. (Cheers.) It is not a party question we are told, and it is not a party question in one high sense, because it is a question of our ,come mon humanity. (Hear, hear.) It is not a party quo. Hon, fer all men, belonging to all parties, ought to have united together in order to protest against these abominable atrocities. We are met with this difficulty, that we can't move a atop in tlee consideration of this question without framing an indictment against her Majesty's Government, for the moment we frame an incliotraent against Her nilajoety's Government, we find all the Tories throughout the kingdom, to a greater or less extent, prepared to back up Her Majesty's Govern. meat through thick and thin, willing to sacrifice these interests of humanity in order to promote the intereste Of their wretched party. (Cheers.) There have been noble exceptions—(hear, hear)—and I am glad to ace knowledge in the various meetings throughout the eountry,that there have been some noble exceptions in which Conservative men of influence have not hesitated to express a decided opinion on this question. (Hear hear.) There have been also in an especial manner noble examples among the bishops and clergy of this nation, and I am glad that the bishops and clergy of the Church of England have stepped forth, and have Shown that they, at all events, in a matter of thie kind, are not prepared to bow their consciences to mere party consideration, but they have pronounced with no uncertain voice against the course pursued by the Government and its officers, and have called on the Government to tale such steps as may be necessary to make reparation for the great injustice that has been committed. These noble men—l say noble because the man is noble who struggles far freedom—(hear, hear)—raised the standard of liberty in the wilds of Herzegovina, and they were prepared to resist the great power of the Turkish Empire' and when they were so standing up in favour of the rights of their countrymen and themselves, instead of re- ceiving sympathy with the Brtiish Government, we had suspicion, we had doubts we had dislike, we had the British Government itself everything In their power to put a stop to these noble men rising for their freedom (Shame.) I ask what has become of the noble boast of the British people that they are in favour of civil and, religions liberty? (Hear, hear.) Sir, I say that is a noble British principle, but I charge on the Government of this country that they have been traitors to this ruling principle of British policy. (Cheers.) Do you remember at the general election of 1874 Mr. Disraeli issued an address in which he said that the Conservative Government would have a "spirited foreign policy." (I. slighter.) A "spirited foreign policy" forsooth I their poli y has been a mean and contemptible policy. (Loud cheers.) It has been worse. It has been a policy that will leave a dark stain on the history, character, and Government of the British people. (Hear, hear.) This has been the spirited foreign policy that Mr. Disraeli's Government have carried out during the last few months. In this appeal which these poor Herzegovinian Bishops and priests made to the A rolibishop of Canterbury, they told the Archbishop that the course which the English Government had taken in allying themselves with the Turkish Government had created amongst that popu- lation a feeling of great hatred towards the English name. They cannot understand how it is that the British people can have acted, through their Govern- ment, in such a manner, as far as possible to defeat the hopes of these Men etruggling for freedom. But, gentlemen, the British Government have got their re- ward. They have made the British name stink in the nostrils of these poor Christians, but it is blest, it is applauded, it is held up, amongst the miserable, wretched,, infamous Turks. An Englishman going amongst tne Turks is received as a brother, he is treated as though he was an intimate ally of the Tur- kish empire, and when a correspondent of the Daily News went to the head quarters of the Turkish army he was received with such shakings of the hand, and each brotherly feeling that he says "I really think i that just now n these parts an idea has gone abroad that the English are a Mahometan sect, differing only on some trilling doctrinal matter from the orthodox believer." (Laughter.) It has come to a nice thing. Don't you think we are indebted to our Government that anyone of us who had happened to go amongst this people who stand in the face of heaven convicted of some of the blackest crimt s that over degraded the human race, would be received as a brother, as a member of the same religious body, only differing on some slight doctrinal opinion: (Shame.) This is what you owe to the policy of the British Government. I have said, and I repeat it, that all this comes of the policy and determination of the British Government to bolster up the Turkish Empire because they fear lest under some conditions, the destruction of the integrity of the Turkish Empire, some advantage will be given to Russia. I have road with great care the Blue Books that have been presented to Parliament, I have per- used this wretched policy of the Foreign Moe during the whole of the correspondence that has taken place train the commencement of the disturbance in Herze- govina, until the last day—which was the middle of August—on which these papers were published. I declare to you that all through these papers there runs this marked determination on the part of the Govern- ment to, if possible, stamp out, or assist in stamping out this insurrection on the part of Herzegovina. There runs through the whole of these papers a feeling on the part of the Government and their age its that there must be no disturbance of the status euo of Tur- key, a feeling which is every now and then expressed, that this " disturbances i " n Herzegovina, as it is called, had been favoured by Russian agents, and that it was intended to subserve Russian policy. The course which the Government hail taken has been all through to get rid of ' what appeared to them a very dangerous element in the East by determining that these things should be kept quiet, no matter how miserable and wretched these people were, and that everybody should have the idea that the Eastern Question was in such a position as to give nobody any trouble at all. On Saturday lest a very important speech was made by Lord Derby explanatory of the conduct of the Government, and in its justification, I have read that speece with great regret and disappoint- ment. Of all the members ef the Tory Government there was no one of whom I had formed so high en opini m as Lord Derby, I remember in former years ha ex. pressed upon this Turkish question itself a very enligh- tened and very advanced opinions, and I was in hopes at all events in his position as Foreign Minister he would take a line which would tend to the advantage of the nation, and at all events he would not in any way be alarmed by this Russian hobgoblin, (Laughter.) He has made a speech whirl in my opinion proves this, if it proves anything that the Uovernment have only given way just to the extent that they have been compelled to give way, and that they will not give way any further unless we contrive to press upon them the fact that the English people are determined they shell give way. (Lad cheers.) I see this morning there is a telegram Irons Berlin in the morning papers, and I observed in that telegram that the correspondent states that "Lord Derby's reply to the deputation created a very unfavpurable impression here,' and the North Gernme Gazette criticises it very severely, and says "if its telegraphic version be correct there i 3 in the tone of the replies a defiance of public opinion in Eng- land and in Europe. His resolution to retain the fleet in Besika Bay is here treated as an act of con- tempt for the harmony of diplomatic action in the im- pending crisis." Ilind lam trespassing on your time —(loud cries of" ge on")—but I should like to say a word about Lord Derby's speech. (Hear, hear.) Be- cause I think we have e right to go to Lord Derby's speech, to see what the Government intend to de, or what at all events their feelings may be. (Hear, hear.) I find first of all that Lord Derby alludes, as other members of the Government have done, to certain. charges which have been brought against the Govern- ment of complicity in these crimes, as if they had been charged with desiring these atrocities to take place. Well, of (sour e, all that is beside the mark. (Hear, hear.) Noboey charges the Government With desiring these atroaities. Nobody supposes the Government would not have gladly prevented these atrocities if they could. (Hear, hear.) That is not the charge, and we have no need to take that matter into our con- sideration, What we do charge the Government with ii this that in regard to these crimes, in the first place they slid not take any proper means of getting to know what was ocauring within a very short distance from Constantinople. And when rumour: reached them in regard to these crimes theyput them aside, and treated them with indifference, and did not in any way at- tempt to follow them up to see if they were true or not, and the Government in connection with the Turkish Government have never, during the whole of the time which these terrible transactions have take place, put that pressure on the Turkish Government which we say they might, and which they ought to have done, and which we believe if they had done they might probably have prevented many of the crimes which have taken place. (Hear, hear,) Lord Derby goes on to argue that they did not know of these atrocities, and he says that even if they had known of them, it was quite clear any steps that might have been taken in regard to sending the fleet to Besika Bay, or in any way supporting the Turkish Govern- meat, could not have had the least effect on the ignorant hordes of miscreants who were guilty of theme atroci- ties in Bulgaria. (Shame.) It is very_easy indeed for Lord Derby to make that assertion. We don't sap- pose that the Bashi-Bazouks were in any way in- fluenced in their minds by the knowledge that the British Government were backing up. Turkey. These horrible wretches knew nothing, 1 dare say, either about the British Government or about any other matter of international polity, but they had been set on by the Turkish Government themselves, arid they knew all about it very well. (Loud cheers.) It was the Turkish Government that had let loose these wretched Bashi Balonks and Circassian% men of no feeling and with no common sense of humanity; and I say, and firmly believe, that if the Government Of this country had not shown such a strong sympathy with 1 Turkey in her past career, and more recently in those diplomatist transactions with Hertegovina, I feel quite sure that Turkey never would have ventured to let loose those horrible, lot mous people on the poor defeneeless inhabitants of Bulgaria. (Loud cheers.) Lord Derby says they did not know anything, and if they had, they would have been quite willing to menet, if possible, to their utmost in bringing this matter to a ssaisfsetory solution. ('. Gammon.") He says the fact of their not agreeing with the IBerlin note was not a proof of their indifference to assist in bringing about pacification, but only proved that they did not approve of the mode in which the note was prepared. It was a very good reason If they could not agree to assist Russia and Germany, to say " We don't exactly agree with your plan, but let us see if we can't get another plan." (Hear, hear.) Instead of that, they said" We won't have your plan, and we won't suggest any other plan." And mark, what was their great objection to it ? That in their judgment it would have been of greater service to the insurgents than to the Govern- ment of the Sultan. (Shame.) In fact, their great object was to take care no measure should be adopted which would be of the slightest service to the insur- gents against the Sultan's Government. I venture to say that, without any fear of contradiction. (Hear, hear.) In the Bias Books a great part of the cor- respondence has reference to this matter, and it is clear that the Government of this country were stalk- ing, by every means in their power, to prevent Benin, M ' Montenegro. and Bosnia assisting the insurgents of. Herzegovina. But what was the consequence of our refusal to agree to the Berlin note ? It was this, that the Turkish Government, knowing it had England at its back, refused to entertain it, It was not formally presented, but it was intimated that the proposal would not be accepted. As soon as that refusal was made known, or in a ishort time at ter- wards, Berrie and Montenegro, people of the IMMO race and blood, and of the same religion as the Hared- govinians and Bosnian entered into the contest and declared war against Turkey. I don't like war my- self, but I am disposed to think it Scotland was saner:, mg under a similar yoke to Herzegovina, or to w on she suffered from the hands of Turkey, I should have been prepared to join in a war in rd. of _overnmenmy fellow- i Christians against the oppressor. G The evidently' supposed these people were pushed forward by the influence of Russia. and not from any goairso to support their fellow Christians. With Out going into all the points, which is unnecessary. because I think the speech of Lord Derby is open to exe6piion in almost every Itue-o(haars heltr- I With to polio out especially tri this epeeoh that although 40 the atrocilles have been broug_ht under the notice of th- GoVernMent, and proved to dereeeseraesee, Lot-A Derby oats the part of an apologist for the Govern- ment of 00 flititttllt So says that they U. bound to girl MARI OA 44% rilik t#l4 ACM ti TOM

and that the barbarities were not in any sense winked at or encouraged at Coostantinople. I can only say, -gentlemen, that this statement is entirely contrary to the fact, utterly contrary to the correspondence of the Blue Books laid before Parliament, and utterly con- trary to the come which the Turkish Government have taken after the atrocities had been committed. (Loud cheers.) It was well known in Constantinople what was taking plaoe in Bulgaria; the Government were in communication with the district of Bulgaria where those atrocities had actually takenplace. (Hear, hear.) Don't suppose for a moment that there was any difficulty of communication between Constanti- nople and Phillipopolis. There were railways and telegraphs. Dna% the Turkish Government know anything about it, think you P I have in my pocket an e :tract from a correspondence with the Turkish Government, sent as an opy!ial communication to the _

British Government on this very subject.,--sign- Resohid Pasha," who Wks the foreign minister of Turkey, and addressed "To Mussuurs Pasha," the ambassador of Turkey in England. I want you, gen- tlemen, to bear with me for a moment in answering the statement of Lord Derby, that these atrocities were in no sense winked at nor enomraged at Constanti- nople. Resehid Pasha writes this letter, in order that it may be laid before Lord Derby. and it is printed in the Blue Book, just laid on the table of the House of Commons, and dated May 14th, the day when these i atrocities n the main had been completed. It was just at the beginning of May and up to the middle of May that these poor creatures were destroyed, and so brutally treated in the way, the newspaper accounts have made known to us. No doubt the Turkish Go- vernment knew all about it—C" Of eourse")—and they wrote to the Turkish Ambassador here—" You have learnt by means of papers that troubles have lately ' arisen on the side of Tartar Bassidjik, a district of Philippolis, although these trouble were far from having the importance whioh malevolence has tried to attribute to them as forming a Bulgarian insurrection, nevertheless, the Government has exerted itself to take from the first energetic and effectual measures suitable to the occasion. These measures have happily pro- dared the results which were justly to be expected from them. The disturbances have had limits set to them from the first, and at present they tend to sub- side." Effectual measures ! Sixty or eighty villages burnt, thousands of men massacred, women and chi'. dren flayed alive, and cast into the flames !—(Shame) all sorts of inhumanities practised, and this the Turkish Government. which, in the language of Lord Derby, has not in any sense winked at nor enooaraved at Constantinople. this Itsashid Pasha, wretched Pasha as he m—(cheers)—strokes his beard and thanks Allah that the mea- sures exerted by the Government have been effectual and suitable for the occasion. (Loud cries of "Shame.") This is not all. The very men who committed these atrocities, the generals in command of the army, and the officers of the Government, have been rewarded, . _

&mended with marks of hononi land, of course, they were so decorated because they had taken these mese sures, which were effectual for the occasion. (Shame.) When we call on the Government to stop this, when we say that we hold them responsible, insomuch as they are sanctioned by the Government, how are we met ? It has no compassion. Even Lord Darby tried to imitate his chief, Mr. D:araeli, by attempting a little wit. (Shame.) It is wonderful how Co eie lamberts of the Tory Utsbinet gat into a jocular humour when they are talking about these frightful occurrences. Lord Derby said What can we do ? you may joist as well suppose that Lord 'eaconsfield was the Sultan and that lam his Grand Vizier." (Laughter.) I dare say, but it is not necessary for these gentlemen to be either Sultans or Prime Ministers. It I. only necessary for tk se gentlemen to feel the pulse of England, and to say to Turkey, in the voice of the English people, 4' Hitherto we have protested your interest, but now It must oome to an end." (Cheers.) Lord Derby says we have no more right to interfe e than France or Germany, or any other great Power, and he says that neither the French, Germans, nor Italians are crying cut and denoueciag their Governments. leo, why not P Because their Governments have done every. thing they could in the matter to atop the war. Ger. many, against whom there can be no charge of having any interested motives, has been foremost in every measure, willing to adopt any plan' or joie any scheme which would tend to lessen the frightful events which are marring in con- sequence of this war. That Government never did ref nee to join in signing the Berlin memorandum, and it had shown a disposition to adopt means by which, this carnage might cease, (Hear, hear.) What hse the British Government done ? The Brit:eh Government is the only Government, which in the transactions that have occurred, has refrained fr en ex- pressing its hatred of the barbarities against the in- habitants of these provinces, and the Germans and Italians, and others denounce our Government as being parties to these great crimes, inasmuch as we did nothing to stop them. Then Lord Darby says that they have adopted a line of "strict neutrality," but non-intervention means destruction to the Herzegoe viniaae. (Hear, hoer.) Ault consider here there is a small population fighting for its freedom, against an empire of twenty or thirty millions of inhabitants, and it was his strict neutrality to say "We will allow ne one to help this little struggling people but we will allow them to be crushed by this gigantic power, whatever the consequence and the resalt may be." And when Semi& and Montenegro joined Herzegovinia, they adopted precisely the same policy. Throughout the Whole of these transactions they had been keeping a ring. Suppose you saw sme little diminutive child fighting with a great big lusty fellow, whose fist was line a sledge hammer, and all you people were to say " Let's have a fight. Let's keep a ring, and see this great bulky fellow with his sledge hammer fist crack this little child's skull." That woad be keeping a ring, and Lard Derby has been keeling a ring. (Loud cheers.) I believe firmly if Great Britain or the Government had been sincere in their sympathy with these struggling nationalities, there would have been a settlement of this question long ago, but the Turkish Government knowing that it could fall back upon the English Government for support, was resolved to resist better counsel and fight to the death against these nationalities, which are struggling to gain their freedom. Lord Derby at the close of his speech says we must not ask the Govern- ment to do impossibilitiee, and says "it is all very well to talk about philanthropy, which is a good thing in its way, but we must bear in mind that foreign powers and politicians are not looking at the question from a philanthrophio point of view." So there comes outthe whole feeling which he supposes operates upon the other foreign powers, and that they have some Moot which induces the British Goverambet to look with great suspicion on anything they propose, and which will lead. the British Government to hesitate about joining them in any movement which, in their judge . ment would interfere with the integrity and position et Turkey. He charges us to be careful, because he says if we take a certain cause against these Mussels men, we may perhaps make them eventually worse, and have a greater amount of carnage, &rod it would result in the Mahornetans. all over the world fighting against the christiana. Therefore he would have us to deal leniently with these atrocities lest worse should follow. Is that the spirit of Englishmen. ("No.") Are you going to be cowed, and afraid. of doing right simply because Lord Derby says there will be !something worse if you do? (" No.") Are you prepared to hold your hand simply because- you have threats as of this kind? (Loud cries of "No.") The threat is baseless as the wind, there are no such prospects. It is only necessary for the Government tO be genuine and sincere in its policy, and I believe the whole thing would become right. (Hear, hear.) Let the Government say they have no jealousy nor sus- picion of Rumis, and that we are willing to act with the other Great Powers in soaring freedom for the in- habitants of Bosnia, Bulgaria, and Herzegovina!, and you will find that there will not be very great difficulty In bringing matters to a satisfactory Conclusion. (Hear. beer.) Don't you be misled by anything less. (Hear, hear.) Don't you be inislei by Lord Derby and the Government into trusting the promises of the Sultan again. The whole of the Blue Book is fell of gross lies on the part of the rurkish Government sad oftici dm They will give any amount of undertakings, but they never think ef fulfilling any of the under. takings they have promised. The Turkish Govern- ment would have no nesitstion in bow-atringing fifty of them Pashas if by. that means they could secure an their provinces. These men would go to their death cheerfully as a public) and patriotic duty, and f eel it was their fate which was reserved te them, and if the ' Turkish Government could blind our eyes with the punishment of these offenders no doubt they would be perfectly satisfied. That is not what we want. (Hear, hear.) The great offender is the Turkish Government itself, and these men are only the wretched instruments of its violence and its tyranny. (Hear, hear.) ENGLISH DUTY IN THE EAST. Ow Wednesday night the people of War- rington joined in the great national protest which is being made against the dastardly crimes committed by the Turks in their European dependencies. ,The Public Hall was filled by an audience of working-men and others; the speakers were inspired with genuine sympathy, and the proceedings were honourable to all who took part in them. It would be unjust to the numerous manifestations of feeling on the Eastern question, to ascribe them to any sentiment less noble and disinterested than a natural abhorrence of cruelty and inhumanity. In the words of Mr. Lowe, uttered on the same evening at a meeting held at Croydon, the issue is too large, too solemn and too momen- tous, to be degraded to the use of any party , emergency. To treat the Eastern question as a party question, would be unfair alike to an adminietration which has simply inheri- ted the traditions of former administrations, and to the millions of Englishmen whose hearts have beaten with a unison ouly so perfect, because it was not preconeerted. If in Warrington, local leaders of the Liberal party have seemed more eager than others that the town should contribute its remons- trance, this unsought distinction has been thrust upon them by the apathy of its lead- ing representatives in the municipality. ' Warrington is probably the only town .in England where an indignation meeting has been held on the Turkish question, which has not been convened and presided over by townsmen identified with the local Government. We do not believe that it is anything but an unhappy accident that the municipal representatives of Warrington are indifferent on the subject of this butchery, we cannot believe that there is less aggre- gate human nature in Warrington than else- where But it is impossible to shut ,ne's eyes to the feet that the Tories in Warring- ton, in whatever they do, betray the em- barrassment of people who feel themselves inferior or unequal to the work to be done. Whether this embarrassment is expressed by the occasional language which is also used by people in the dark, to convince themselves that they are not afraid, or whether it is expressed by inopportune silence, and inaction, the effect is always the same. however, let us dismiss even the suggestion that in Warrington some persons have allowed considerations of party to pre- dominate over the natural impulse to en- deavour to influence our Government in such a way that an end shall be put to the fright- ful outrages of the Turks. At all events let us not dwell unnecessarily on the fact that the men of Warrington, who, in virtue of their official .and representative character, should have been the first to espouse and advocate a noble cause, seems to have stul- tified their better feelings in obedience to some small and miserable party sentiment. The speech of Mr. Bylands—an authoriseel report of which we publish elsewhere—was chiefly directed against the tone adopted by Lord Derby in his replies to the rece .t depu- tations to him on the Eastern difficulty. While we cordially agree with his protest against the formal and somewhat heartless utterances of Lord Derby, it is but fair to the Foreign Secretary to bear in mind that he is only pursuing a policy which has be- come traditional, and for which one party is as much responsible as the other. The old legend about the balance of power in Europe has probably done more harm than any other silly fable. 'he very words " balance of power " are a contradiction in terms. You cannot balance power, because power is pre- dominant. The relative martial strength of the six great uropean nationalities can be pretty closely computed, and tne value of their geographical positions can be ascer- tained precisely. IN4 ow the solution of the Eastern difficulty is the reply to this ques- tion. If we drive the Turks out of Europe, who is to possess or control the present in- surgent dependencies? No one would seriously maintain that the acquisition of those provinces would materially affect the relative strength of any one of these six great powers. But because we have been jealous of the possible designs of hussia in another quarter, it has been our policy to maintain the integrity of Turkey, on the transparently absurd ground that we were maintaining the balance of power in Europe, Zr. Rylands wisely exposed the puerility of this Russian bug-bear tradition, and when that is disposed of, we are bound to act like a responsible wit- nem to a deed of outrage. That by our unwise and selfish protection of Turkey twenty years ago, and the pecuniary help we heve since given her, we have encour- agedto entertain a false sense of gfi !ntervention in her the .Part. it eiall the more jscuialrT affsecauirrist,yrefnrodmersfo nt upon us to undo the mischief, acknowledge our error, and shew ourselves to iurkey in our true character—the friends only of liberty, justice, and civilisation. It has, perhaps, been too much our ambition, as a nation, to act as the policeman of the world, and to attempt feats of chivalry beyond our strength. Both native and foreign satirists are fond of representing us as people who miss seeing and succouring much of themisery at our doors, in our eager gaze at the distant object of sympathy. div.head: TURKS,
div.p: THE TURKS,

The national hatred of wrong and of bar- barous treatment of the weak, as illus- trated so terribly in the Turkish behaviour in Bulgaria, continue day by day, to deepen in intensity and to spread through our Eng- lish towns and cities like a conflagration. The columns of the daily newspapers are crowded with reports of the proceedings of public assemblies convened to express by grave and formal resolutions the general de- testation of the crime and bloodshed by which the track of the Turkish soldiery is marked and branded as with a scourge. The sympathy of the ,country,—expressed indi- vidually and collectively—witnesses no abatement; and the records of horror which have sunk indelibly into the mind of the nation are bearing their natural fruit in the storm of remonstrance and indignation that is ringing in the ears of the British Govern- ment, The long catalogue of remonstrance which every day receives notable and im- pressive additions can only be barely indica- ted ma journal like ours, but brief indica- tions suffice to show the extent and force of the general feeling. That the military crimes of the Turks show litle sign of abatement may be gathered from a commentary offered ; by way of a reply to a note just issued by the Ottoman Embassy, which, on the part of its Government, is adding a mendacious hypocrisy to its crimes of butchery and rapine. A note issued by the Ottoman Embassy states that "the Ottoman Government, obeying sentiments of humanity, hes agreed to extend to the rebellion it is now repress- ing the provisions of the compact of Geneva; although in its eyes those provisions are obligatory only in international wars." The chiefs of corps are, as far as this depends on Ottoman armies, to endeavour to make re- ;Tooted the stipulations of the Convention of Geneva, and it is by these express instruc- tions that the troops in the field are strictly regulating their conduct. A practical com- ment upon these humanitarian professions Is supplied, with singular and quite acci- dental unanimity by the correspondents of the Times, Daily News, and Standard. Three Servian prisoners were roasted to death, and their charred bodies were seen by an Eng- lish correspondent in the neighbourhood of Alexinatz. Other traces of "atrocious cruelty" to tie wounded are said to be well authenticated. The Ciroassians are reported to be burning every village in the Morava Valley south of Deligrad. The Standard'. correspondent, the tone of whose previous letters is sufficient to free him from the sus- picion of hostility to the Turks, o affirms these reports, and adds another horrible detail to the hideous story by referring to girls out- raged and flayed alive by the Turkish irregular cavalry. Minister Ristios seems to have some warrant for stating in his Note to the diplomatic agents that "the whole Turkish mode of proceeding is one inexor- able system of persistent persecution, de- struction, and extermination, and not the mode of warfare carried on by civilised nations."

One has a preference for the statements of the correspondents of Conservative journals, who, at any rate, are likely to be free from any desire to exaggerate crimes, the details of which it is supposed may embarass the Government which they are supposed to have taken un- der their protection. A brief telegram from the Standard is full of Turkish character and "colour." The Standard's Belgrade corres- pondent telegraphs that during and after Friday's battle the Turks committed great atrocities. Hideous stories reach . him of rape and murder, of wounded Russians tied to trees and roasted alive, of girls brought into the Bervian camp after a cavalry raid still breathing, but flayed alive, after being subjected to outrages, compared with which mere murder is a venial offence. The Tur- kish march to Krujevatz and Kujazevatz may be descried at night by the glare of burning villages. There is no force between the Turks and Belgrade. After statements of this kind it seems idle to dream that it is likely, that the red-handed —or as Mr. Gladstone would say—the "red- handed and red-armed" barbarians of the Turkish army can ever experience any com- punction for the deeds they have perpe- trated.

This modern means of locomotion appears to be growing in favour with the young men of England, and remarkable journeys are often made on these ap- parently fragile vehicles. The bioyclists started from Altrineham at 6-80 a.m., anci at a pleas eight miles on the Altrincham side of Chester they breakfasted staying an hour. They then continued their journey to Wrexham Which place they reaohed at half-past eleven, having travelled 421 miles. On Tuesday evening the massive 18. carat gold chain and badge made by Elkington and Co., to which i 5 appended a gold locket bearing the arras of Sir Gil- bert Greenell, Bart., and M.P., was formally presented by Lady Greenell with whom the idea is supposed to have originated. The presentation took place at the Town Hall, where the members of the corporation and their friends had ariembled to meet Sir Gilbert and his lady, and to receive Messrs. Elkington's specimen of art manufact are. Champagne and grapes were handed round to grace the occasion, the Mayor presiding. In presenting this elegant souvenir from the House of Greenall to the corporation Lady Gramma said: "Mr. Mayor,—lt is with real pleasure that I have come down this evening to present this chain and badge to you. It has been my own idea. It is ray sincere wish that you will like it, and associate it only with kindly feel- ings, for my sake. I have the interest and happiness of the Corporation and the people of Warrington at heart."

Her Ladyship then gracefully proceeded to put the new oollar on his Worship, who accammodated himself to the operation with corre- sponding grace, amidst a visible flutter of amiable excitement on the part of the ladies.
